title: Desktop app
text: Downloads — builds for Windows, macOS and Linux. Desktop app guide — installation, registration, permissions and updates.

title: Self-hosting
text: TolkTak can run on your own hardware or a rented server. Requirements Install with Docker Install from source

title: Configuration and maintenance
text: Configuration — environment variables and LiveKit settings. Administration — registration, invites and access. Upgrades and backups — saving and restoring data. Troubleshooting — connections, audio and service logs. TolkTak is in early development. Back up server data before upgrading. There is no end-to-end encryption yet: the server operator has access to stored messages and files. See the security model for details.

title: Development
text: Architecture , building and testing , HTTP and WebSocket API . The guides are also available on the website and in Russian .

title: Installation
text: System Build Windows 10 and 11, x64 .exe macOS, Apple Silicon or Intel .dmg for your processor Linux, x64 .AppImage or .deb Download the app

title: Registration and sign-in
text: Open the server address in a browser and create an account. If registration is invite-only, the operator will need to provide an invite code. Start TolkTak and enter the same server address, username and password. The registration button in the app opens the selected server's website in a browser. Each server has its own accounts. Example addresses: https://talk.example.com — a server with HTTPS; http://192.168.1.20:8080 — a server on a local network without HTTPS. Use your server's address in place of these examples. A self-signed certificate also needs to be trusted on the device.

title: Permissions
text: The app requests microphone and camera access when they are first used. If access is denied, the voice and video settings display a warning with a link to system permissions. On macOS, screen sharing requires separate permission under Privacy & Security. TolkTak may need to be restarted after changing it.

title: Platform differences
text: System Screen-sharing audio Windows 11 Audio from the selected app when sharing a window. When sharing the entire screen, call participants' voices are excluded from system audio. Windows 10 All system audio, including call participants' voices. The app displays a warning before sharing. macOS and Linux Video without audio. Push to talk works outside the TolkTak window on Windows. On macOS and Linux, it requires the app window to have focus. Global hotkey support on Linux with Wayland depends on the desktop environment.

title: Updates
text: New versions are available on the downloads page . In builds that support automatic updates, the app downloads the new version and offers to restart. Automatic updates are not available on macOS yet; new versions need to be installed manually. For sign-in, audio and screen-sharing issues, see Troubleshooting .

title: Server
text: The Docker setup requires: Linux on x86-64 or ARM64; Git, Docker Engine and the Compose plugin; access to network and firewall settings; storage for the database, uploaded files and backups. The standard setup runs two services: TolkTak and LiveKit. SQLite is included; PostgreSQL can be configured separately. An installation from source requires Python 3.14, uv and LiveKit Server instead of Docker. That guide covers the versions and installation steps.

title: Load
text: Memory, CPU and bandwidth use depend on concurrent connections and media streams. Minimum CPU and RAM requirements have not been established yet. LiveKit forwards streams to participants. If five people watch one screen share, the server receives one stream and sends five copies. The server's outbound bandwidth matters when choosing a connection.

title: Addresses
text: Setup Addresses and connectivity Internet server with HTTPS Two host names, a public IP or port forwarding, a reverse proxy and certificates. Local network without HTTPS An IP address or host name that participants can reach. Each service uses its own port. See Domains and addresses for setup. In HTTP mode, passwords, messages and files are sent without encryption.

title: Ports
text: Default values from the project's configuration: Port Protocol Purpose 443 TCP HTTPS through the reverse proxy 80 TCP Certificate validation via HTTP-01, if used 8080, 7880 TCP Direct access to TolkTak and LiveKit in HTTP mode 7881 TCP Media for connections where UDP is unavailable 50000–60000 UDP Voice, video and screen sharing 3478 UDP TURN 30000–40000 UDP TURN relay With HTTPS, ports 8080 and 7880 listen only on 127.0.0.1 . LiveKit media ports need to be opened separately: port 443 alone is not enough for calls. See Firewall and ports for example rules and port changes.

title: Desktop app
text: See the desktop app guide for supported systems and platform differences. Once the server is ready, follow Install with Docker .

title: Install with Docker
text: Docker Compose runs the TolkTak server and LiveKit for voice, video and screen sharing. This guide assumes a Linux server with Git, Docker and the Compose plugin installed. See Requirements for hardware and network ports.

title: 1. Deployment files
text: git clone https://github.com/D4eNst/tolktak.git cd tolktak/deploy Run all subsequent commands from the deploy/ directory.

title: 2. Configuration
text: The init.sh script creates .env with server parameters and livekit.yaml with LiveKit settings. It generates fresh keys when run. These files contain secrets and should not be published. HTTPS requires two domain names pointing to the server: one for TolkTak and one for LiveKit. ./init.sh talk.example.com lk.example.com Replace the example domains with your own. In this configuration, both services listen on 127.0.0.1 ; a reverse proxy handles HTTPS with certificates for both names. Calls also require open media ports . For a setup without HTTPS, pass the machine's address that participants can reach: ./init.sh --http 192.168.1.20 With this address, TolkTak is available at http://192.168.1.20:8080 and LiveKit at ws://192.168.1.20:7880 . Passwords, messages and files are sent over unencrypted HTTP. For an internet server, use the HTTPS setup above. The main settings are in .env : Parameter Purpose TOLKTAK_SERVER_NAME Server name. TOLKTAK_REGISTRATION Registration mode. The default is invite . The first account can be created in any mode. TOLKTAK_VERSION TolkTak image version. The default is latest ; a specific tag pins the version. Other settings are listed in the configuration reference . If .env already exists, init.sh stops rather than overwriting it. Edit existing configuration files directly.

title: 3. Start the services
text: docker compose up -d docker compose ps Compose downloads ghcr.io/d4enst/tolktak-server with the selected tag and starts both services. To view their logs: docker compose logs --tail 100 tolktak livekit

title: 4. Create the administrator
text: After starting the server, register at its address, for example https://talk.example.com or http://192.168.1.20:8080 . The first account becomes the administrator , so create it straight away. The administration panel is at /admin on the same address. It provides invites for other participants. They register on the server's website and sign in to the desktop app with the same server address, username and password.

title: 5. Check the connection
text: Use two accounts to check app sign-in, messaging, a call and screen sharing. A participant connecting from another network helps verify media port access: a working chat alone does not confirm it. For voice and video connection issues, see Troubleshooting . After the first launch, set up backups .

title: Install from source
text: This runs the server from a checkout under systemd, without Docker. Use it when you want to run a specific commit or cannot use containers.

title: 1. Install the server
text: The server is a Python application. It needs Python 3.14 and uv , which installs the dependencies and, if the system has no Python 3.14, Python itself. curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh # or see the uv documentation for other ways sudo git clone https://github.com/D4eNst/tolktak.git /opt/tolktak cd /opt/tolktak/server sudo UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR=/opt/tolktak/python "$(command -v uv)" sync --no-dev This creates a virtual environment in server/.venv with the tolktak-server command in server/.venv/bin/ . UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR keeps a Python downloaded by uv under /opt/tolktak , where the service user can read it, rather than in root's home directory. The website is part of the package. By default the server keeps its data in SQLite; to use PostgreSQL, see PostgreSQL . A source install reports its version as 0.1.0-dev . To show the real one, write it into tolktak/_version.py before starting: echo "__version__ = \"$(git describe --tags --always)\"" | sudo tee tolktak/_version.py

title: 2. Install LiveKit
text: Download livekit-server 1.13 for your architecture from the LiveKit releases and install it to /usr/local/bin/ .

title: 3. Generate the configuration
text: The same init.sh as for Docker writes both files. Run it in deploy/ and move the results: cd /opt/tolktak/deploy sudo ./init.sh talk.example.com lk.example.com # or: ./init.sh --http 203.0.113.10 sudo mkdir -p /etc/tolktak sudo mv .env livekit.yaml /etc/tolktak/ .env does not set the listen address and data directory, which Docker Compose otherwise supplies. Add them to /etc/tolktak/.env , using 0.0.0.0:8080 as the listen address if you run without a certificate: TOLKTAK_LISTEN=127.0.0.1:8080 TOLKTAK_DATA_DIR=/var/lib/tolktak LIVEKIT_INTERNAL_URL=http://127.0.0.1:7880

title: 4. Create the services
text: sudo useradd --system --home /var/lib/tolktak --create-home tolktak sudo chown root:tolktak /etc/tolktak/.env /etc/tolktak/livekit.yaml sudo chmod 640 /etc/tolktak/.env /etc/tolktak/livekit.yaml /etc/systemd/system/tolktak.service : [Unit] Description=TolkTak server After=network-online.target livekit.service Wants=network-online.target [Service] User=tolktak WorkingDirectory=/opt/tolktak/server EnvironmentFile=/etc/tolktak/.env ExecStart=/opt/tolktak/server/.venv/bin/tolktak-server Restart=on-failure [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target /etc/systemd/system/livekit.service : [Unit] Description=LiveKit media server After=network-online.target Wants=network-online.target [Service] User=tolktak ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/livekit-server --config /etc/tolktak/livekit.yaml Restart=on-failure LimitNOFILE=65536 [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl enable --now livekit tolktak journalctl -u tolktak -f

title: 5. Finish
text: With HTTPS, set up the reverse proxy . Then open the server's address and register the administrator account, as described in Install with Docker . To upgrade: cd /opt/tolktak/server sudo git checkout tolktak/_version.py # only if you wrote the version into it sudo git pull sudo UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR=/opt/tolktak/python "$(command -v uv)" sync --no-dev sudo systemctl restart tolktak Database migrations run on start.

title: With HTTPS: two host names
text: In the standard setup, TolkTak and LiveKit run on the same machine with separate host names. The reverse proxy routes requests to the appropriate service. Name Record type Value talk.example.com A 203.0.113.10 lk.example.com A 203.0.113.10 The names and IP above are examples. Use your own domains and the server's public address. Only add an AAAA record when IPv6 is configured; otherwise some devices may try an address that cannot be reached.

title: Check DNS
text: dig +short talk.example.com A dig +short lk.example.com A For records without proxying, both commands should return the server's public IP. DNS changes may take time to appear. Pass the same names to the setup script: TolkTak first, then LiveKit. ./init.sh talk.example.com lk.example.com

title: DNS provider proxying
text: This guide assumes direct connections to the server. With a provider that offers a CDN proxy, use DNS only for both names. In this mode, DNS returns the server's own address; see Cloudflare's documentation . LiveKit media ports and TURN must be reachable directly. An ordinary HTTP proxy does not forward UDP traffic.

title: Without a certificate: one address
text: A local network setup can use one address with separate ports: http://192.168.1.20:8080 — TolkTak; ws://192.168.1.20:7880 — LiveKit. Generate the configuration for this example with: ./init.sh --http 192.168.1.20 Replace 192.168.1.20 with your machine's address. HTTP sends passwords, messages and files without encryption. For internet access, continue with HTTPS certificates , then the reverse proxy .

title: HTTPS certificates
text: HTTPS protects passwords, messages and files in transit between a device and the server. In the TolkTak setup, certificates are installed on the reverse proxy.

title: Trusted certificate
text: An internet server needs a trusted certificate for each of the two host names . One certificate can also cover both names. nginx: obtain and renew certificates through an ACME client such as Certbot. Let's Encrypt issues free certificates. Caddy: automatic issuance and renewal for domains in its configuration. When configuring an ACME client, domain validation methods include: Method Requirements HTTP-01 The domain points to the server; port 80/TCP is reachable from the internet. DNS-01 A TXT record in DNS. Works with port 80 closed and supports wildcard certificates. See Let's Encrypt's documentation for details. Renewal should be automatic; nginx needs to reload its configuration after a certificate is replaced.

title: Self-signed certificate
text: A closed network can use a certificate from a private certificate authority. This requires trust to be configured separately on every participant's device. The certificate must list the server name or IP in the Subject Alternative Name field. The app does not disable certificate checks: an untrusted chain, a name mismatch or an expired certificate prevents connection.

title: No certificate
text: HTTP mode is available for local networks: ./init.sh --http 192.168.1.20 Use your machine's address here. Passwords, messages and files are sent over unencrypted HTTP. Voice and video between the app and LiveKit are protected by DTLS-SRTP; TolkTak does not implement end-to-end encryption yet. Continue with Reverse proxy for HTTPS routing.

title: Reverse proxy
text: In the HTTPS setup, the proxy accepts requests on port 443 and forwards them to local services. It holds the certificates; TolkTak and LiveKit listen on 127.0.0.1 . Host name Local address talk.example.com http://127.0.0.1:8080 lk.example.com http://127.0.0.1:7880 This example uses the default ports. If the ports change in the project configuration, update the proxy addresses too. Media streams reach LiveKit through separate ports .

title: nginx
text: Download the example configuration The same file is in the repository at deploy/nginx.conf.example . It configures both host names, WebSocket forwarding and the upload limit. Add the example to the nginx configuration, for example /etc/nginx/conf.d/tolktak.conf . Replace the domains, local ports and certificate paths. Check and apply the configuration: sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx The systemctl command applies to a system using systemd. The example uses http2 on from nginx 1.25.1 and later; this line can be removed on earlier versions.

title: Main parameters
text: Parameter Purpose Upgrade , Connection WebSocket forwarding for chat events and call connections. client_max_body_size Request body limit. The example sets 60m for a TolkTak file limit of 50 MB. proxy_read_timeout Time to wait for service data: 120 seconds for TolkTak and 3600 for LiveKit in the example. X-Forwarded-For Participant address for request rate limiting. When changing TOLKTAK_MAX_UPLOAD_MB , keep the nginx limit higher to allow for request overhead. Requests over the limit return HTTP 413. See nginx's documentation for WebSocket forwarding. Use TOLKTAK_TRUST_PROXY=1 when TolkTak can only be reached through a trusted proxy.

title: Check the setup
text: curl https://talk.example.com/healthz Use your own domain. An ok response confirms that TolkTak is reachable through HTTPS. Test a call and screen sharing separately with two accounts, preferably on different networks. Other proxies need the same service addresses, WebSocket support and an appropriate upload limit. For connection problems, see Troubleshooting .

title: Firewall and ports
text: Open these ports for incoming traffic. The numbers are defaults; init.sh prints the ones it configured. Port Protocol Needed for 443 TCP HTTPS on the reverse proxy (HTTPS layout). Port 80 too, if your certificate client uses HTTP-01. 8080 and 7880 TCP TolkTak and LiveKit directly (layout without a certificate) 7881 TCP Media over TCP, for clients whose network blocks UDP 50000–60000 UDP Media. This is the main path for voice and video. 3478 UDP TURN, for clients behind strict NAT 30000–40000 UDP TURN relay Example with ufw : sudo ufw allow 443/tcp sudo ufw allow 7881/tcp sudo ufw allow 50000:60000/udp sudo ufw allow 3478/udp sudo ufw allow 30000:40000/udp Also open the same ports in your hosting provider's firewall or security group, if it has one; that one is easy to forget.

title: Changing the ports
text: Pass different numbers to init.sh in the environment, for example on a shared server: TOLKTAK_PORT=18480 LIVEKIT_PORT=17880 RTC_UDP_START=55000 RTC_UDP_END=55499 \ TURN_RELAY_START=55500 TURN_RELAY_END=55999 ./init.sh talk.example.com lk.example.com init.sh writes them to both .env and livekit.yaml . To change them later, move .env and livekit.yaml aside and run init.sh again; it generates a new LiveKit key, so restart the whole stack afterwards. A UDP range of about 500 ports serves a few hundred simultaneous streams. Smaller ranges work for small groups.

title: Behind NAT
text: If the server has a private address behind a router, forward every port above to it, and make sure LiveKit learns the public address: use_external_ip: true in livekit.yaml (the default) discovers it through STUN. On hosts with Docker networks or a VPN, also uncomment rtc.interfaces in livekit.yaml so LiveKit offers only the public interface.

title: PostgreSQL
text: TolkTak stores its data in SQLite by default: one file, tolktak.db , in the data directory, with nothing else to install. It can use PostgreSQL instead. Uploaded files stay in the data directory either way.

title: Which one to use
text: SQLite is the right choice for a quick start, a test server, or a small server for friends. There is nothing to set up, and a backup is a copy of the data directory. PostgreSQL is recommended for a main server that many people rely on. It handles many people writing at once better, it can run on another machine or as a managed service, and it comes with its own tools for backups, replication and monitoring. You can start with SQLite and move later; see Moving an existing server . Databases created by earlier versions of TolkTak open unchanged, and the schema is migrated automatically when the server starts, on both. The server picks the database from TOLKTAK_DATABASE_URL (see Configuration ). Empty means SQLite in the data directory; a postgres://user:password@host:5432/dbname address means PostgreSQL.

title: Option A: PostgreSQL in the same Docker Compose setup
text: Add a postgres service next to TolkTak. Put it in deploy/docker-compose.override.yml , which Docker Compose merges into docker-compose.yml automatically, so git pull does not conflict with your change: services: postgres: image: postgres:17 restart: unless-stopped environment: POSTGRES_USER: tolktak POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD} POSTGRES_DB: tolktak ports: - 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 volumes: - postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data healthcheck: test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U tolktak -d tolktak"] interval: 5s timeout: 5s retries: 10 tolktak: depends_on: postgres: condition: service_healthy volumes: postgres-data: The TolkTak container uses host networking, so it reaches PostgreSQL at 127.0.0.1:5432 , not by the service name postgres . The port is published only on 127.0.0.1 ; change the left-hand 5432 if that port is taken on the host. Generate a password and add both lines to deploy/.env : openssl rand -hex 24 POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<the generated password> TOLKTAK_DATABASE_URL=postgres://tolktak:<the generated password>@127.0.0.1:5432/tolktak A hex password needs no escaping in the URL. If you choose your own, percent-encode characters such as @ , : , / and # . On a new server, start everything with docker compose up -d . On a server that already has data in SQLite, follow Moving an existing server instead, or the server starts with an empty PostgreSQL database.

title: Option B: an existing or managed PostgreSQL
text: Any PostgreSQL the server can reach works: one already running on the host, on another machine, or a managed service from your provider. Create a user and a database for TolkTak with psql as an administrator: CREATE USER tolktak WITH PASSWORD 'choose-a-password'; CREATE DATABASE tolktak OWNER tolktak; The server creates its tables on the first start. Set the address in deploy/.env (or /etc/tolktak/.env for a source install ): TOLKTAK_DATABASE_URL=postgres://tolktak:choose-a-password@db.example.com:5432/tolktak Restart the server. Its tolktak-server listening log line shows database=postgres when it uses PostgreSQL. If PostgreSQL runs on another machine, allow the TolkTak server in its pg_hba.conf and firewall, and nobody else. Keep the database close to the server: network latency to the database adds to almost every request.

title: Moving an existing server
text: tolktak-server copy-db FROM TO copies all data from one database to another. The destination must be empty; the command refuses to write into a database that already has accounts. Uploaded files stay where they are, in the data directory. With Docker Compose, after setting up PostgreSQL as in option A or B: cd tolktak/deploy docker compose stop tolktak docker compose run --rm tolktak copy-db sqlite:///data/tolktak.db \ postgres://tolktak:<password>@127.0.0.1:5432/tolktak Then make sure TOLKTAK_DATABASE_URL is set in .env and start the server with docker compose up -d . Users stay signed in, since their sessions are copied too. For a source install: sudo systemctl stop tolktak sudo -u tolktak /opt/tolktak/server/.venv/bin/tolktak-server copy-db \ sqlite:///var/lib/tolktak/tolktak.db postgres://tolktak:<password>@127.0.0.1:5432/tolktak Add TOLKTAK_DATABASE_URL to /etc/tolktak/.env and sudo systemctl start tolktak . copy-db only reads the data from the SQLite file (after bringing its schema up to date, as the server would on start). Keep the file until you are sure everything works: going back is a matter of removing TOLKTAK_DATABASE_URL , though anything written to PostgreSQL in the meantime stays there. The same command copies in the other direction, from PostgreSQL to an empty SQLite file.

title: Backups
text: With PostgreSQL, a backup has two parts: a database dump and the uploaded files in the data directory. cd tolktak/deploy docker compose exec -T postgres pg_dump -U tolktak -Fc tolktak > tolktak-db-$(date +%F).dump pg_dump takes a consistent snapshot while the server keeps running. Back up the files/ folder of the data directory as described in Maintenance ; files are never modified after upload, so it can be copied while the server runs. For an external or managed PostgreSQL, run pg_dump against it with the same address, or use the provider's backups. To restore, stop TolkTak and load the dump back: docker compose stop tolktak docker compose exec -T postgres pg_restore -U tolktak -d tolktak --clean --if-exists < tolktak-db-2026-01-31.dump docker compose start tolktak With SQLite, by comparison, the database is one file in the data directory and is backed up with it.

title: Tips
text: Pin the major version ( postgres:17 ). A new major version cannot open the old data directory; moving to one takes a dump and restore. Do not publish PostgreSQL on a public interface. With option A it listens only on 127.0.0.1 . Test a restore once, on another machine or into a scratch database. A backup that has never been restored is a guess. The rest of the configuration does not change: LiveKit, the reverse proxy and the apps do not know which database the server uses.

title: Configuration
text: The server is configured with environment variables. With Docker Compose they live in deploy/.env , which init.sh creates from .env.example . With a source install they are in /etc/tolktak/.env . Restart the server after a change: docker compose up -d recreates the container when .env changed.

title: tolktak-server
text: Variable Default Description TOLKTAK_SERVER_NAME TolkTak Name shown in the app and on the website. TOLKTAK_REGISTRATION invite open : anyone can register. invite : an invite code is required. closed : nobody can. The very first account can always register and becomes the administrator. TOLKTAK_MAX_UPLOAD_MB 50 Maximum size of one uploaded file. Keep the reverse proxy's body limit above it. TOLKTAK_CLIENT_DOWNLOAD_URL empty Link to the desktop app on the server's website. Empty hides the button. LIVEKIT_PUBLIC_URL required wss:// or ws:// address the apps use to reach LiveKit. LIVEKIT_API_KEY , LIVEKIT_API_SECRET required Must match keys in livekit.yaml . The secret must be at least 32 characters. LIVEKIT_INTERNAL_URL http://127.0.0.1:7880 Address the server uses for LiveKit's API. Set by the Compose file. TOLKTAK_LISTEN :8080 Listen address. The Compose file builds it from TOLKTAK_BIND and TOLKTAK_PORT . TOLKTAK_DATA_DIR ./data Uploaded files, and the SQLite database when TOLKTAK_DATABASE_URL is empty. /data in the container. TOLKTAK_DATABASE_URL empty Database to use. Empty: SQLite in tolktak.db in the data directory. postgres://user:password@host:5432/dbname (or postgresql://... ) for PostgreSQL, recommended for a main server; sqlite:///absolute/path.db for an SQLite file elsewhere. See PostgreSQL . TOLKTAK_TRUST_PROXY off 1 uses X-Forwarded-For as the client address for rate limits. Enable only when the server is reachable exclusively through your proxy, or clients can spoof their address. TOLKTAK_DEBUG off 1 enables debug logging. The server refuses to start, with a clear message, if a required variable is missing or a value is invalid.

title: Docker Compose only
text: Variable Default Description TOLKTAK_VERSION latest Tag of ghcr.io/d4enst/tolktak-server to run. Pin a release such as 0.1.0 to upgrade only when you choose. TOLKTAK_BIND , LIVEKIT_BIND 127.0.0.1 Interfaces the services listen on. 0.0.0.0 for the layout without a reverse proxy. TOLKTAK_PORT , LIVEKIT_PORT 8080 , 7880 HTTP ports of the two services. RTC_TCP_PORT , RTC_UDP_START , RTC_UDP_END 7881 , 50000 , 60000 LiveKit media ports. Also written to livekit.yaml . TURN_UDP_PORT , TURN_RELAY_START , TURN_RELAY_END 3478 , 30000 , 40000 LiveKit's built-in TURN server. Also written to livekit.yaml . Port variables are read by init.sh when it renders livekit.yaml ; changing them in .env alone does not move LiveKit. See Firewall and ports .

title: livekit.yaml
text: init.sh renders it from livekit.yaml.template . Settings you may want to change: rtc.use_external_ip discovers the public address through STUN. Keep it on for servers on the internet. rtc.interfaces limits which network interfaces LiveKit offers to clients. Useful on hosts with Docker bridges, VPNs or several addresses, where clients otherwise try unreachable candidates first. turn is LiveKit's built-in TURN over UDP, which helps clients behind strict NAT. TURN over TLS on port 443 would need its own certificate and is not configured. webhook.urls must point to the server's /api/v1/livekit/webhook ; it is how the server learns who is in a voice room. See the LiveKit configuration reference for everything else.

title: Administration
text: What the person running a server can control, and what they are responsible for.

title: The administrator
text: The first account registered on a server becomes its administrator, whatever the registration mode. Register it right after the first start, before you share the address. There is one administrator role and it covers the server, not the groups in it: the administrator manages invites and is otherwise a normal user. Groups are run by their own members (see below).

title: Registration and invites
text: TOLKTAK_REGISTRATION decides who can create an account: Mode Use when invite (default) You hand out codes to the people you want. open The server is on a private network, or you want anyone with the address to join. closed Everyone who should be there already is. Invites are managed on the server's website at /admin , signed in as the administrator. Each code has a use limit (1 to 1000) and an expiry in days. Delete a code to revoke it; accounts created with it stay. People register on the server's website; an invite link ( /?invite=CODE ) fills the code in. There is no account deletion or ban in this version. To remove a person, remove them from the groups they are in (group owners and moderators can), and stop issuing them invites.

title: Groups
text: Any user can create a group and becomes its owner. Roles in a group: Member Moderator Owner Chat, voice, screen sharing ✓ ✓ ✓ Rename the group, change its picture and description ✓ ✓ Add members, remove members ✓ ✓ Create, rename and delete voice rooms and text channels ✓ ✓ Remove a moderator, appoint moderators ✓ Delete the group ✓ If the owner leaves, ownership passes to the member who joined earliest. A group disappears when its last member leaves. Limits per group: 200 members, 20 voice rooms, 30 text channels. Messages are up to 4000 characters with up to 10 attachments.

title: Data and privacy
text: Be clear with your users about this: You, as the operator, can read everything stored on the server: messages, files and the account list. There is no end-to-end encryption. Voice and video are not recorded or stored. A file is available to anyone who has its link, without signing in. Links are random and are not guessable. Deleting a message erases its text and its attachment list from the database. The uploaded files themselves stay on disk. See the security model for the details.

title: Server address and name
text: The name shown in the apps comes from TOLKTAK_SERVER_NAME . Users connect by address, so changing domains means everyone has to sign in again with the new address; keep the old name pointing to the server for a while, or redirect it in the reverse proxy.

title: Upgrading
text: Read the release notes first. The database schema is migrated automatically when the new version starts; there is no way back to an older version after that except restoring a backup, so take one first. Docker, prebuilt image. With TOLKTAK_VERSION=latest : cd tolktak/deploy git pull # picks up changes to the Compose file and examples docker compose pull docker compose up -d With a pinned version, change TOLKTAK_VERSION in .env to the new release, then run the same commands. Docker, built from source. git pull docker compose up -d --build Source install. Pull, run uv sync --no-dev and restart the service, as in Install from source . LiveKit is pinned in docker-compose.yml . A new TolkTak release updates the pin when a newer LiveKit is tested; there is no need to update it separately. Users' apps update themselves from GitHub Releases.

title: Backups
text: Everything the server knows is in its database and its data directory: tolktak.db (SQLite, the default) and the files/ folder with uploads. Back them up together with deploy/.env and deploy/livekit.yaml . With PostgreSQL, the data directory holds only files/ ; back up the database with pg_dump as described in PostgreSQL . The simplest consistent backup stops the server for a moment: cd tolktak/deploy docker compose stop tolktak docker run --rm -v deploy_tolktak-data:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \ tar czf /backup/tolktak-data-$(date +%F).tar.gz -C /data . docker compose start tolktak The volume name is <directory>_tolktak-data ; docker volume ls shows it. For a source install, archive /var/lib/tolktak the same way. For SQLite backups without stopping, use SQLite's online backup ( sqlite3 tolktak.db ".backup backup.db" ) and copy files/ afterwards; files are never modified after upload. Restore: stop the server, extract the archive into an empty volume or data directory, restore .env and livekit.yaml , start the server. With PostgreSQL, restore the database dump before starting.

title: Logs and health
text: docker compose logs -f tolktak docker compose logs -f livekit curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz # "ok" For a source install, use journalctl -u tolktak -f . Set TOLKTAK_DEBUG=1 to get more detail while you investigate a problem.

title: Moving to another machine
text: Back up as above, install on the new machine with the same .env and livekit.yaml , restore the data, then point DNS at the new address. Users stay signed in, since their sessions are in the database.

title: Renewing certificates
text: Certificates are renewed by whatever issued them (see HTTPS certificates ). Reload the reverse proxy after renewal if your certificate client does not do it for you.

title: Troubleshooting
text: Start with the logs: docker compose logs --tail 100 tolktak livekit .

title: The server does not start
text: The log names the problem: a missing LIVEKIT_API_KEY or LIVEKIT_API_SECRET , a secret shorter than 32 characters, a missing LIVEKIT_PUBLIC_URL or an unknown TOLKTAK_REGISTRATION value. "address already in use" means another service has the port; pick another as described in Firewall and ports .

title: The app cannot connect to the server
text: Open the server address in a browser on the same device. If the page does not load, the problem is DNS, the firewall or the reverse proxy, not the app. Certificate errors: the app accepts only certificates the system trusts. A self-signed certificate must be installed as trusted on that device; see HTTPS certificates . Without a certificate, type the address with the scheme and port: http://203.0.113.10:8080 . Without a scheme, the app assumes https:// for public addresses.

title: Chat works, voice does not
text: This is almost always the media path. Connection to LiveKit fails right away. Check LIVEKIT_PUBLIC_URL : it must be reachable from the user's device, with wss:// behind HTTPS and ws:// without a certificate. Open https://lk.example.com in a browser; LiveKit answers "OK". Joins, but nobody hears anybody, or it drops after about 15 seconds. UDP ports are blocked. Open them in both the server's firewall and your provider's firewall; see Firewall and ports . The LiveKit name is proxied by a CDN. Media cannot go through it. Turn the proxy off for that name; see Domains and addresses . Works for some users only. Users on strict networks need port 7881/TCP or TURN (3478/UDP and the relay range). On hosts with several interfaces, set rtc.interfaces in livekit.yaml . The room list shows people who already left. The LiveKit webhook does not reach the server. Check webhook.urls in livekit.yaml ; the server also corrects the list every 20 seconds.

title: Uploads fail
text: "File is too large" with HTTP 413 comes either from the server ( TOLKTAK_MAX_UPLOAD_MB ) or from the reverse proxy ( client_max_body_size in nginx). The proxy's limit must be higher than the server's.

title: The app keeps reconnecting
text: The WebSocket is being closed by something between the app and the server. Check that the proxy passes WebSocket upgrades and that its read timeout is above 70 seconds; see Reverse proxy .

title: Reporting a bug
text: Open an issue with the server version ( /api/v1/server shows it), the app version and system, and the relevant log lines. Remove addresses and names you do not want to publish. Security problems go through SECURITY.md instead.

title: Architecture
text: This page describes how TolkTak is put together, for people deploying or changing it.

title: Components
text: Desktop client (Electron) ├─ main process: window, tray, global hotkeys, screen and audio capture, updates ├─ preload: a small allow-listed IPC bridge └─ renderer: Preact UI, REST and WebSocket client, livekit-client │ │ │ HTTPS: REST API │ WebRTC media: UDP, TCP or TURN │ WSS: event stream │ WSS: LiveKit signalling ▼ ▼ tolktak-server (Python, ── join tokens ──▶ LiveKit SFU SQLite or PostgreSQL) ◀── webhooks ────── Path Contents server/ tolktak-server : REST API, WebSocket events, the website (registration, invite management), LiveKit token issuing and webhook handling. Python 3.14 with FastAPI on Uvicorn and Tortoise ORM; SQLite or PostgreSQL. client/ The Electron app: src/main (main process), src/preload (IPC bridge), src/renderer (UI, TypeScript and Preact). client/e2e/ End-to-end tests against a real LiveKit and server, and Windows capture checks. deploy/ Docker Compose deployment with LiveKit, configuration templates and an nginx example. The server is the source of truth for users, groups, channels, voice rooms, messages and files. It stores everything in one database, with uploaded files in the data directory on disk, and migrates the schema on start. The database is SQLite in WAL mode by default, or PostgreSQL when TOLKTAK_DATABASE_URL points to one; both hold the same schema, and tolktak-server copy-db copies all data from one to the other. It runs as a single asyncio process (Uvicorn with uvloop) and is organised in a few modules: api/ holds the REST and WebSocket handlers, store/ the database access for users, groups, chat and files, realtime.py the hub that fans events out to connected clients, and livekit.py the token signing, webhook verification and calls to LiveKit's API. The realtime hub and the rate limits live in memory, so the server is meant to run as one process per database. Clients talk to it over a REST API under /api/v1/ and receive changes (new messages, edits, reactions, typing, presence, voice room occupancy, calls) over one WebSocket per client. The server sends an application-level ping every 25 seconds; the client treats 70 seconds of silence as a dead connection and reconnects with exponential backoff, then fetches the messages it missed. Sending a message is idempotent: each message carries a client-generated nonce, and the server keeps one message per author and nonce, so a retry after a dropped connection does not create a duplicate. LiveKit is a selective forwarding unit (SFU): it receives each participant's audio and video once and forwards it to the others without mixing or transcoding. It knows nothing about users or groups. Every group voice room and every direct-message call maps to one LiveKit room. LiveKit reports participants joining and leaving through webhooks, which the server uses to show who is in which room. Every 20 seconds the server also lists the participants of active rooms through the LiveKit API, so a lost webhook does not leave stale state.

title: Media path
text: The client asks the server to join a room. The server checks that the user is a member of the group (or of the direct-message channel) and returns a LiveKit access token for that room, valid for 12 hours. The client connects to LiveKit with that token and publishes its microphone, camera and screen share. LiveKit forwards the tracks to the other participants over DTLS-SRTP. When UDP is blocked, media goes over TCP or through LiveKit's built-in TURN server. Voice. Microphone audio passes through a processing chain in an AudioWorklet before it is sent: optional neural noise suppression (RNNoise, GTCRN or DeepFilterNet3, compiled to WebAssembly), then a high-pass filter, a voice leveller, a compressor, a look-ahead limiter and a gate for voice activity or push-to-talk. All of it runs locally on the CPU. DeepFilterNet only recognises speech at normal recording levels, so its input is raised towards about -24 dBFS and its output lowered by the same amount. Voice is sent as Opus with DTX and RED. Speaking indicator. Each client measures levels itself 20 times a second: remote voices from the decoded audio, its own voice from the output of the processing chain. The ring turns on at once and off after 450 ms below the threshold. LiveKit's active-speaker events are smoothed on the server and arrive late, so they are only a fallback. Video and screen sharing. Camera and screen tracks are published with simulcast, so LiveKit can send a lower layer to viewers on slow connections instead of slowing everyone down. H.264 is used when the system can encode it, VP8 otherwise, with no second backup codec. A screen share has its full layer and one layer of exactly half its size, so that both stay on the hardware encoder (Chromium encodes odd sizes and anything below 360p in software). "Source" quality, and sources too small for a half-size layer of at least 360p, go out as a single layer. The client chooses what it receives itself rather than from the size of the video element. The watched stream gets the full layer, and previews of other streams get the 360p layer. While the window is in the background, behind a game, previews and cameras are not received and the interface does not animate. This can be turned off in the settings. Screen sharing has two modes: one keeps the frame rate and lowers resolution under pressure (video and games), the other keeps resolution and lowers frame rate (text and code). Screen sharing audio. On Windows 11 the client uses WASAPI process loopback: when sharing a window, it finds the process that owns the window and captures only that process tree's audio; when sharing a whole screen, it captures all system audio except TolkTak's own process tree, so the other participants' voices are not sent back to them. On older Windows versions only full system loopback is available, which includes the voices of the room; the app warns about this before sharing. macOS and Linux share video without audio. Stream audio is sent as stereo Opus at up to 160 kbit/s without voice processing, DTX or RED, and only viewers who opened the stream subscribe to it.

title: Security model
text: The server is designed to be run by people who trust its operator. The operator can read everything stored on it. What is and is not encrypted. Client-server traffic is protected by TLS on your reverse proxy (plain HTTP when the server runs without a certificate), media by DTLS-SRTP between each client and LiveKit. There is no end-to-end encryption: LiveKit handles decrypted media, and messages and files are stored unencrypted in the data directory. Accounts. Passwords are hashed with Argon2id (3 iterations, 64 MB, 2 threads). Login returns a random 256-bit bearer token; the database stores only its SHA-256 hash. A session lasts until the user logs out. The WebSocket connection authenticates with the token in its first frame, so tokens do not appear in URLs or proxy logs. The first account on a server becomes the administrator. Depending on TOLKTAK_REGISTRATION , new accounts need an invite code created by the administrator; codes have a use limit and an expiry date. Rate limits. The server applies per-key token-bucket limits to registration and login (per client address and, for login, username), password changes, sending messages, reactions and uploads. Behind a reverse proxy, TOLKTAK_TRUST_PROXY=1 makes it use X-Forwarded-For as the client address. Access control. Messages, channels, rooms and voice tokens are only available to members of the group or direct-message channel. LiveKit tokens are scoped to one room. LiveKit webhooks are accepted only with a valid signature from the configured API key and a matching body hash. Uploaded files. Uploads are limited by TOLKTAK_MAX_UPLOAD_MB and stored under a random 128-bit identifier, not under their original name. The content type is detected from the file's contents rather than taken from the client. Only common image, audio and video types are served inline; everything else is served as a download with application/octet-stream . Every file response carries Content-Security-Policy: sandbox and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff , so an uploaded file can never run as a page of the server's origin. File downloads do not require a session: anyone who has a file's URL can fetch it. Website. The pages served by the server use a strict Content Security Policy ( 'self' only) and cannot be framed. Desktop client. The renderer runs with sandbox and contextIsolation enabled and Node.js integration disabled, under a Content Security Policy, and can reach the main process only through an allow-listed bridge. Navigation away from the app is blocked. The session token is encrypted at rest through Electron safeStorage (DPAPI on Windows, the Keychain on macOS, the Secret Service keyring on Linux). Where no keyring is available, it is stored in a file readable only by the user. Electron fuses disable RunAsNode , NODE_OPTIONS and the inspector flags, and enable ASAR integrity validation and loading the app only from the ASAR archive. Copy-protected content. TolkTak does not bypass DRM. Windows that display protected video may be captured as a black image.

title: Prerequisites
text: Python 3.14 and uv (see server/pyproject.toml ; uv can install Python for you) Node.js 22 and npm LiveKit server 1.13 ( livekit-server binary), for running a local stack and the end-to-end tests Docker, only if you want to test the deployment

title: Repository layout
text: Path Contents server/ Python server, package tolktak . __main__.py is the tolktak-server entry point and app.py builds the FastAPI application; api/ (HTTP and WebSocket handlers), store/ and db.py (database access and schema migrations, SQLite or PostgreSQL), realtime.py (WebSocket hub), livekit.py (tokens, webhooks, API calls), web/ (website), copydb.py (the copy-db command). Tests are in server/tests/ . client/src/main/ Electron main process: window, tray, hotkeys, screen and audio capture, updater. client/src/preload/ The IPC bridge exposed to the renderer. client/src/renderer/ UI ( ui/ ), voice and video ( voice.ts , audio/ ), API client, translations ( i18n/ ). client/e2e/ Playwright end-to-end tests. tools/voice-scores/ DNSMOS, PESQ and STOI thresholds for voice-quality.spec.ts . perf/ CPU and memory regression runs of the client on Linux ( perf.yml ). deploy/ Docker Compose deployment. See Architecture for how the pieces fit together.

title: Server
text: cd server uv sync uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check . && uv run ty check uv run pytest The tests use a temporary SQLite database and need no external services. To run every test against PostgreSQL as well, point TOLKTAK_TEST_POSTGRES at a database you can use for that: TOLKTAK_TEST_POSTGRES=postgres://tolktak:secret@127.0.0.1:5432/tolktak_test uv run pytest The release version is written into tolktak/_version.py when the Docker image is built (build argument VERSION ); a checkout reports 0.1.0-dev .

title: Running a local stack
text: Chromium ignores loopback ICE candidates, so LiveKit must advertise a real network address of your machine, even when everything runs locally. Replace 192.168.1.20 below with your LAN address. Create livekit-dev.yaml outside the repository: port: 7880 bind_addresses: ["0.0.0.0"] rtc: tcp_port: 7881 port_range_start: 50000 port_range_end: 50200 use_external_ip: false node_ip: 192.168.1.20 keys: devkey: dev-secret-0123456789abcdefghijklmnop webhook: api_key: devkey urls: ["http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/livekit/webhook"] Start LiveKit and the server in two terminals: livekit-server --config livekit-dev.yaml cd server TOLKTAK_REGISTRATION=open \ LIVEKIT_API_KEY=devkey \ LIVEKIT_API_SECRET=dev-secret-0123456789abcdefghijklmnop \ LIVEKIT_PUBLIC_URL=ws://192.168.1.20:7880 \ uv run tolktak-server The server listens on :8080 and keeps its data in server/data/ . Open http://localhost:8080 to register the first account. All server variables are listed in Configuration .

title: Client
text: cd client npm ci npm start # build once and launch Electron Enter localhost:8080 as the server address. Addresses on localhost and private networks default to http:// , everything else to https:// . Script What it does npm run build Bundle main, preload and renderer into dist/ with esbuild npm run watch Rebuild on every change; run npx electron . in another terminal and restart it to pick up changes npm start Build and launch the app npm run typecheck Type-check the whole client with tsc npm run test:e2e Run the Playwright tests (see below) npm run dist:win Build the Windows NSIS installer and zip into release/ (run on Windows) npm run dist:win:zip Build only the portable Windows zip (works from Linux) npm run dist:mac Build macOS .dmg and .zip for arm64 and x64 (run on macOS) npm run dist:linux Build the Linux AppImage and .deb Environment variables for the client: Variable Used by Effect TOLKTAK_DEFAULT_SERVER build Prefills the server address on the login screen, for builds made for one community NODE_ENV=production build Minifies the bundle and drops source maps TOLKTAK_USER_DATA app Uses a different profile directory, so several instances can run side by side TOLKTAK_NO_UPDATES app Disables the update check in a packaged build Releases are built by .github/workflows/release.yml when a v* tag is pushed: it builds the installers for all three platforms, publishes them to GitHub Releases, and pushes the server image to ghcr.io/d4enst/tolktak-server .

title: End-to-end tests
text: The tests in client/e2e/ start a real stack: they start tolktak-server from server/ on port 18080, start livekit-server with a generated configuration on ports 17880 and 17881, and serve the renderer bundle from client/dist on port 18090. Nothing on the server side is mocked. Media assertions look at real decoded frames, audio levels and RTP statistics, not at what the UI shows. cd client npm run build LIVEKIT_BIN=/path/to/livekit-server npx playwright test Notes: LIVEKIT_BIN points to the LiveKit binary. CHROMIUM_PATH selects a Chromium build instead of the one Playwright installs ( npx playwright install chromium ). The specs that launch Electron ( electron.spec.ts , audio.spec.ts , chat.spec.ts ) need a display. On a headless Linux machine, run them under xvfb-run -a . The network-loss tests in resilience.spec.ts drop traffic with iptables and must run as root. The test locale is ru-RU and the specs look up Russian UI labels, so keep both translations in sync when you change a string the tests use. long.spec.ts is a long watch-together session, skipped unless LONG_MIN=<minutes> is set. E2E_VERBOSE=1 prints the server and LiveKit logs. These run in CI and can be run locally the same way: voice-quality.spec.ts , voice-worklet.spec.ts and denoise.spec.ts render the shipped noise suppressors offline. With uv installed, voice-quality.spec.ts also scores the output with tools/voice-scores/score.py against thresholds.json (run uv sync --project ../tools/voice-scores once). voice-cpu.spec.ts measures the CPU cost of each preset in Electron; on Linux run it under xvfb-run -a . perf/ci.sh starts the stack with real Electron clients, measures idle and call scenarios and checks them against perf/baseline/ci-linux.json . It needs LIVEKIT_BIN , the server environment ( uv sync in server/ ) and Xvfb. A single run: perf/run.sh voice --clients 2 --duration 40 . client/e2e/windows.spec.ts checks screen sharing on a real Windows PC: that a shared window's audio reaches viewers without the voices of the room, and which video encoder is actually used. It runs only on Windows with TT_API set. Install the server and download LiveKit: cd server uv sync --no-dev Put livekit-server.exe from the LiveKit releases into the same bin\ folder at the repository root. Start the stack from the repository root. The script picks your LAN address, writes the configuration and database to data\ , and prints the API address: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File client\e2e\windows\start-stack.ps1 Build the client and run the tests: cd client npm ci; npm run build $env:TT_API = "http://<lan-ip>:8080" npx playwright test e2e/windows.spec.ts Results are written to windows-results.json , gpu-results.json and hw-results.json in client/ (or in TT_RESULTS_DIR ). client/e2e/windows/windows-probe.ps1 is a read-only script that collects the Windows build, CPU, GPU and driver, displays and audio devices into tolktak-probe.txt on the desktop. Attaching its output helps when reporting capture problems.

title: HTTP and WebSocket API
text: The desktop app uses this API, and so can your own tools and scripts. It is a JSON API under /api/v1 . Stability. The API is not versioned beyond /v1 yet and may change between minor releases while TolkTak is at 0.x. Check the release notes before upgrading a server that your scripts depend on. client/src/renderer/api.ts is the reference client and always matches the server of the same version.

title: Conventions
text: Requests and responses are JSON ( Content-Type: application/json ), except file uploads and downloads. Timestamps are Unix milliseconds. IDs are integers, except file IDs, which are random strings. Errors have an HTTP status and a body of the form {"error": {"code": "invite_invalid", "message": "Invite code is invalid, expired or used up"}} . code is stable and meant for programs; message is English text for people. Rate-limited requests get 429 with code rate_limited .

title: Authentication
text: POST /api/v1/auth/login {"username": "alice", "password": "…", "device": "my-script"} returns {"token": "…", "user": {…}} . Send the token on every other request: Authorization: Bearer <token> A token is valid until POST /api/v1/auth/logout . POST /api/v1/auth/register takes username , display_name , password and, in invite mode, invite . For automation, create a separate account for the script, so its token can be revoked without affecting a person.

title: Endpoints
text: Method and path Description GET /server Server name, version, registration mode, LiveKit address. No authentication. POST /auth/register , /auth/login , /auth/logout Accounts and sessions. GET /me , PATCH /me , POST /me/password Own profile ( display_name , about , status , avatar ) and password. GET /users All users on the server. GET /channels Channels the user is in: direct messages and group text channels, with the last message and unread count. POST /dms Open a direct-message channel with user_id . GET /channels/{id}/messages History. Query: before , after , limit , q (search). POST /channels/{id}/messages Send: text , nonce (client-generated, makes retries safe), optional reply_to and attachments (file IDs). POST /channels/{id}/read Mark read up to message_id . PATCH /messages/{id} , DELETE /messages/{id} Edit or delete own message. POST /messages/{id}/reactions Toggle the reaction emoji . POST , DELETE /messages/{id}/pin ; GET /channels/{id}/pins Pinned messages. POST /files?name=… Upload; the body is the raw file. Returns {"file": {"id", …}} . GET /files/{id}[/{name}] Download. No authentication; see security model . GET /groups , POST /groups , PATCH , DELETE /groups/{id} Groups. POST /groups/{id}/members , DELETE /groups/{id}/members/{uid} , PUT /groups/{id}/members/{uid}/role Membership and roles. POST /groups/{id}/channels , PATCH , DELETE /text-channels/{id} Text channels. POST /groups/{id}/rooms , PATCH , DELETE /rooms/{id} Voice rooms. POST /voice/join , POST /voice/leave Get a LiveKit URL and token for room_id (group room) or channel_id (direct call). POST /calls/{channel}/ring , /decline , /cancel Direct-message calls. GET , POST /admin/invites , DELETE /admin/invites/{code} Invites. Administrator only. Paths in the table are relative to /api/v1 . GET /healthz (outside /api/v1 ) returns ok for health checks.

title: Events
text: Open a WebSocket to /api/v1/ws and send the token as the first frame within 10 seconds: {"type": "auth", "token": "…"} The token is never put in the URL, so it does not end up in proxy logs. The server answers with hello (your user, who is online, current voice rooms, server name and version) and then pushes events as {"type": "…", "data": {…}} : Event When message.created , message.updated A message was sent, edited, deleted, reacted to or pinned. channel.created , channel.deleted , channel.read Channels appeared or disappeared; read position changed on another device. group.updated , group.deleted Group settings, members, rooms or text channels changed. user.created , user.updated , presence Accounts and online status. typing Someone is typing in a channel. voice.room Who is in a voice room, with mute, deafen, camera and screen flags. call.ring , call.declined , call.cancelled , call.ended Direct-message calls. ping Every 25 seconds. Treat 70 seconds without any frame as a dead connection. Events tell you that something changed; after a reconnect, fetch what you missed through REST ( GET /channels , then messages?after=… ). A client can send {"type": "typing", "channel_id": …} .

title: Voice
text: POST /voice/join returns a LiveKit url , token and room . Connect with any LiveKit SDK to publish or subscribe to audio and video. Tokens are scoped to that one room.

title: Bot API (planned)
text: There is no dedicated bot API yet. Today a script can act as a regular user through the API above. Planned for a later version: bot accounts created by the administrator, with tokens that do not expire with a login session and are marked as bots in the app; per-bot permissions instead of full user rights; outgoing webhooks for events, as an alternative to holding a WebSocket open; slash commands registered by bots. Ideas and use cases are welcome in issues .

title: Supported versions
text: TolkTak is in early development. Security fixes are made in the latest release only; please upgrade the server and the desktop app before reporting.

title: Reporting a vulnerability
text: Please do not report security vulnerabilities in public issues, discussions or pull requests. Report them privately through GitHub: open the Security tab of the repository and choose Report a vulnerability . Include: the affected component (server, desktop app, deployment files) and version; a description of the problem and its impact; steps to reproduce, or a proof of concept; any suggested fix, if you have one. You will get a response within 7 days. We will keep you informed while we work on a fix, agree on a disclosure date with you, and credit you in the advisory unless you prefer not to be named.

title: Scope
text: The security model describes what TolkTak protects against and what it does not. At present, a server operator can read the messages and files stored on their server, media is not end-to-end encrypted, and files can be downloaded by link without authentication. These are limitations of the current version; reports about these documented limitations are not vulnerabilities, although proposals to improve them are welcome as issues.

title: Contributing to TolkTak
text: Thank you for your interest in TolkTak. Bug reports, fixes, features and translations are all welcome.

title: Before you start
text: For bugs, search the existing issues first, then open a new one with the bug report template. For larger changes or new features, open an issue to discuss the idea before writing code. It saves everyone time if the direction needs adjusting. For questions and ideas that are not yet a concrete proposal, use GitHub Discussions . Security problems are reported privately: see SECURITY.md .

title: Development setup
text: See Building and testing for prerequisites, running a local stack and the end-to-end tests. Before opening a pull request, run the same checks as CI: cd server && uv sync && uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check . && uv run ty check && uv run pytest cd client && npm ci && npm run typecheck && npm run build

title: Pull requests
text: Keep each pull request focused on one change, and describe what it changes and why. Add or update tests for the behaviour you change. Server changes need tests in server/tests/ (pytest); client changes that affect behaviour need an end-to-end test where one is practical. Changes to the media path (voice, camera, screen sharing, stream audio, watch-together) are accepted only with an end-to-end test that checks the real stream, such as decoded video frames, audio levels or RTP packet statistics, not just the presence of elements on screen. Follow the style of the surrounding code. Python code is formatted and linted with ruff ( uv run ruff format . ). Update the documentation in docs/ when you change behaviour, configuration or deployment. Every string shown to users goes through the translation files (see below), never inline in a component.

title: Translations
text: UI strings live in client/src/renderer/i18n/ . English ( en/ ) is the reference; every other language is a directory that mirrors it file by file, and each file is typed against its English counterpart, so a missing or misspelled key is a compile error. To add a language: Copy client/src/renderer/i18n/en/ to a new directory named after the language code, for example de/ . In each file, import the English module's type and declare the object with it, as the existing ru/ files do: import type en from '../en/chat'; const de: typeof en = { // ... }; export default de; Translate the strings. Strings that depend on a number or a name are functions; keep their parameters. Register the language in client/src/renderer/i18n/index.ts : add it to the Locale type, the LOCALES list (with the language's own name), the dictionary map, and the locale detection and intlLocale functions. Run npm run typecheck in client/ . It fails until every string is present. The pages served by the server ( server/tolktak/web/static/ ) are translated separately: each page script ( index.js , admin.js , docs.js ) holds its own en and ru dictionaries, and i18n.js switches between them.

title: Code provenance and licensing
text: Write your own code. Do not copy code from projects whose license is incompatible with AGPL-3.0-or-later, and do not submit code derived from decompiling or disassembling proprietary software. If you add a dependency or bundle third-party assets (models, sounds, fonts, images), state its license in the pull request. It must be compatible with AGPL-3.0-or-later. By submitting a contribution, you agree that it is licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 or later , the license of the project.
